prompt.context: Your client is Walter Black Industries, a privately owned chemical manufacturing company based in Albuquerque, New Mexico that specializes in producing car wash chemicals. The client has two major products, Car Wash A and Truck Wash A. After a series of aggressive acquisitions 5 years ago, the client has become a market leader, but revenue growth has become stagnant in the last 2 years.
prompt.question: The client would like us to identify opportunities to increase revenue by 30% without reducing profit margins.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current revenue and profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: The client made $1B last year (60% from Car Wash A, 40% from Truck Wash A) with a profit margin of 40%. The client would like to keep overall profit margins across all products at or above 40%.

clarifying_info.q: What does the client sell and who handles distribution/packaging?
clarifying_info.a: The client only sells chemicals. The customer pays for all distribution and packaging costs.

clarifying_info.q: How has the industry been growing?
clarifying_info.a: The car and truck wash chemicals industry has been growing by 2% on average over the last 10 years. It is difficult for both the customer and end customer of the product to differentiate between product quality.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have new products in the pipeline?
clarifying_info.a: The client currently has no new products in the pipeline. Formulations for new products take 5 years to develop and have a high chance of failure (85%).
The client only sells to chemical wholesale distributors. The client sells to the top 5 wholesale distributors who control 95% of the global market share.

clarifying_info.q: Are there concerns about new market entrants or acquisition targets?
clarifying_info.a: Capital costs are high and there are no concerns over new market entrants. No potential acquisition targets are available.
There are three main competitors for the client. Along with the client, these four companies control 90% of the entire market.

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side bar charts comparing Revenue, Cost, and Profit for Walter Black Industries and Competitors A, B, C — one chart for Car Wash Chemicals and one for Truck Wash Chemicals.

data.car_wash_revenue_scale: 0 to ~1,600 $M axis; Walter Black Industries and competitors shown with stacked cost/profit bars
data.truck_wash_revenue_scale: 0 to ~800 $M axis; Walter Black Industries and competitors shown with stacked cost/profit bars

exhibits.title: Pricing Analysis
exhibits.shows: A table showing current pricing and volume data for Car Wash A and Truck Wash A — price per gallon, cost per tote, average annual totes sold, and average annual revenue.

framework: Revenue growth levers: price vs. volume
Price: current pricing vs. competitor pricing, elasticity of demand, room to raise or lower prices
Volume: market share gains, customer expansion (sell to more distributors), geographic expansion
New products/services: pipeline feasibility (constrained — 5 year lead time, 85% failure rate)
New markets: adjacent chemicals or industries
Profit margin check: any revenue lever must keep overall margin at or above 40%

questions.prompt: What insights can you derive from Exhibit 1 (Competitive Benchmarking)?
questions.guidance: Strong candidate identifies: (1) Client has ~20% dollar market share in car wash category and has significantly higher margins than competitors; (2) Client has ~20% dollar market share in truck wash category but significantly lower margins than competitors; (3) The car wash chemicals revenue pool is roughly 50% larger than the truck wash pool; (4) The cost component is a distractor — costs are similar among competitors, so margin differences are driven by pricing, not cost. Candidate should pivot to pricing as the key revenue lever.

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 2 and the elasticity data below, what is the optimal pricing strategy for Car Wash A and Truck Wash A? (Car Wash A: $1 change in $/gal changes demand by 50,000 totes; Truck Wash A: $1 change in $/gal changes demand by 100,000 totes. Totes are 200 gallons. Prices can only change in $1 increments.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must find the price that maximizes revenue for each product independently. Two valid approaches: (1) build a price-quantity-revenue table stepping through $1 increments; (2) derive a formula and take the derivative. Optimal: decrease Car Wash A to $8/gal, increase Truck Wash A to $6/gal. Note: simply raising Truck Wash A to $5, $6, or $7 is a valid simplified answer that also meets the goals.

math.setup: Revenue = Price x Quantity x 200 gal/tote. Demand is linear. Car Wash A baseline: $10/gal, 300K totes. Each $1 change in price changes demand by 50K totes (opposite direction). Truck Wash A baseline: $2/gal, 1,000K totes. Each $1 change changes demand by 100K totes (opposite direction).
steps: Car Wash A formula: Q = 800 - 50P (derived from baseline: at P=10, Q=300K; slope = -50K per $1). R = P x 200 x Q = 200P(800-50P) = 160,000P - 10,000P^2. dR/dP = 160,000 - 20,000P = 0 => P = 8. Or equivalently R($M) = 800P - 50P^2 (in $M with totes in thousands); dR/dP = 800 - 100P = 0 => P = 8.
Truck Wash A formula: Q = 1200 - 100P (derived: at P=2, Q=1000K; slope = -100K per $1; intercept = 1000+100*2=1200). R($M) = 1200P - 100P^2; dR/dP = 1200 - 200P = 0 => P = 6.
Table approach — Car Wash A: P=$7->$630M, P=$8->$640M (peak), P=$9->$630M. Truck Wash A: P=$5->$700M, P=$6->$720M (peak), P=$7->$700M.
New total revenue = $640M + $720M = $1,360M. Revenue growth = $1,360M / $1,000M = 136% > 130%. Goal met.

Profit check — Car Wash A: revenue per tote=$1,600, cost per tote=$1,000, profit per tote=$600, totes=400K => profit=$240M. Truck Wash A: revenue per tote=$1,200, cost per tote=$300, profit per tote=$900, totes=600K => profit=$540M. Total profit=$780M. Margin=$780M/$1,360M=~57% > 40%. Goal met.
math.answer: Optimal pricing: Car Wash A at $8/gal (down from $10), Truck Wash A at $6/gal (up from $2). New revenue = $1,360M (+36%). New profit margin ~57%. Both goals achieved.

recommendation: Decrease Car Wash A price from $10/gal to $8/gal and increase Truck Wash A price from $2/gal to $6/gal. This pricing strategy increases total revenue by 36% to $1.36B while raising profit margins from 40% to approximately 57%, meeting both client objectives.
risks: Competitor reaction: lower prices on Car Wash A could trigger a price war that erodes margins
Lowering Car Wash A price may negatively affect brand perception given the client's market-leader positioning
Significant price increase on Truck Wash A ($2 to $6 is a 3x increase) may cause customer pushback or volume loss beyond modeled elasticity
next_steps: Coordinate with sales team to implement new pricing with customers
Perform additional customer segmentation analysis to determine whether differentiated pricing by customer could further improve revenues
Monitor competitor responses and build contingency plan if price war emerges
